Editor’s note: This story is no longer being updated. Read the latest updates on the Republican primary for Colorado governor here.

First-time candidate Victor Marx took a narrow lead over state Sen. Barb Kirkmeyer early Wednesday evening as counties uploaded more results in the race for the Colorado Republican Party’s gubernatorial nomination.

Marx’s margin stood at 2,262 votes as of 7:40 p.m., according to the Associated Press. Marx led 39.9% to Kirkmeyer’s 39.4% with just over 500,000 votes tallied so far, according to the AP. Rep. Scott Bottoms, a conservative pastor from Colorado Springs also seeking the GOP nomination, was in third with 20.7%.

The AP estimated about 92% of votes in the race had been counted. Should the final margin in the race fall within 0.5% of the leading candidate’s vote total, Colorado law requires an automatic recount.

Kirkmeyer had led in results since polls closed Tuesday night and then all day Wednesday, by narrowing margins.

But around 5 p.m., El Paso County — a Marx stronghold — and Denver, where she’s led, were among counties began updating their results for the day after counting tens of thousands more ballots, resulting in an overall shift in Marx’s favor. The AP projected more outstanding ballots were left to count in El Paso County than in Denver, which was nearing completion. But other counties that favor Kirkmeyer, including Arapahoe County, still expected to report more, too.

Kirkmeyer has led in several Front Range counties, including the red-tinted Douglas County. She had fallen behind in Adams County and trailed in El Paso County, a conservative stronghold.

Shortly before Marx took the lead, his spokesman, Roger Hudson, said the campaign felt confident that late votes would continue to break for Marx and that he would overtake Kirkmeyer.

“We feel more confident (now) than we did even last night, after seeing the numbers coming today,” he said.

In an interview late Wednesday morning, when she still was leading, Kirkmeyer said she, too, was optimistic about her chances. She pointed to outstanding ballots in Front Range counties where she had led Marx.

"We peaked pretty much at the right time, the momentum is behind us, the trend is coming our way," she said.

Nearly 400 people gathered for Marx's watch party at a ranch-resort in Larkspur on Tuesday night, and by 8:45 p.m., they were milling about as country music played and a projector screen showed the results. Marx spoke well after 9 p.m., telling his supporters that while he remained confident he would win, final results would likely not come Tuesday night or, potentially, on Wednesday.

"So it is too close to call tonight," he said, though "every drop of more votes, they're leaning toward us."

"We've kept pressing forward because the mission is simply to win and get our state back," he continued.

If Kirkmeyer ends up winning, she will have successfully steered the party away from Marx and Bottoms' more religious conservatism in favor of a more mainstream Republican politics. A state senator and longtime Weld County commissioner, Kirkmeyer has for years been among the most prominent Republicans in a state that has become dominated by Democrats.

The assumed front-runner when she entered the race last year, she promoted her candidacy as a balance to Democrats' legislative control over the past eight years. She pitched herself as an experienced hand who was ready to step in and address the state's fiscal woes. Though out-fundraised by Marx, she garnered more support from the party's traditional and moderate wing, who viewed her as the most viable approach to win back power -- or at least limit down-ballot losses -- in a blue state.

Still, she faced an unexpected challenge from Marx, a nonprofit leader with an extensive history. He describes himself as a high-risk humanitarian, and the nonprofit he runs -- which provides training to law enforcement and trauma support for people -- had annual revenues surpassing $7 million in 2024.

But he's also claimed to have killed a man as a child and to have exposed and removed demons from people. Unlike Kirkmeyer, whose strength has long been her policy chops, Marx ran a campaign focused primarily on direct outreach to voters, premised on his own charisma and Republican voters' distaste for established candidates.

Whoever wins the race for the GOP nomination will face long odds in November. Colorado has not elected a Republican to the governor's mansion in more than 20 years, and the state has only become more electorally inhospitable to the GOP in the years since.

In the Democratic race, Attorney General Phil Weiser beat U.S. Sen. Michael Bennet for his party's nomination. Regardless of whether Kirkmeyer or Bottoms prevails, Weiser will be heavily favored to win the general election in November and succeed Gov. Jared Polis, who is term-limited.

The Republican winner will also have to try to unite a fractured Colorado GOP. During the campaign, Kirkmeyer and Bottoms said they would not support Marx should he become the party's nominee, and they accused him of being a con man and a fraud. A spokesman for Kirkmeyer said Tuesday that she still did not intend to support Marx should he win.
